solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Native poet’s back in Italy more than once (7)

annotation.definitionNote: Native stands for a native of Israel; the clue leans on the rest of the sentence to supply the country

indicatorNotes.back: the poet's name is read back to front
indicatorNotes.in: the turned name sits inside the two Is

blocks.note: I is the international code for Italy; the first of two
LEAR'S, the nonsense poet Edward Lear's, turned round
Italy used a second time, I again

annotation.surface: A native poet seems to keep going back to Italy, visit after visit.
annotation.walkthrough: 'More than once' tells you to use Italy's I twice, one on each side. Edward Lear is the crossword's favourite poet; his name with its 's turns into SRAEL.
annotation.definitionFit: An Israeli is a native of Israel, though 'native' alone is a thin definition, as solvers on the day remarked.

entries.clue: Correspondence of form is second rising art movement (11)

indicatorNotes.rising: in a down clue, rising means reading upwards, so MO turns round

blocks.note: MO, a second or moment, written upwards
Orphism, the colourful abstract style of Robert Delaunay

annotation.surface: A critic notes that a rising art movement shares its form with another.
annotation.walkthrough: Orphism is an obscure offshoot of Cubism, so the last seven letters may need the definition first. 'Second' is MO, as in 'wait a mo'.
annotation.definitionFit: Isomorphism is identity or close similarity of form, in crystals, organisms or mathematical structures.

entries.clue: Magistrate is concerned with always finishing early (5)

indicatorNotes.finishing early: the word stops one letter before its end

blocks.note: re = concerning, as in a memo heading

annotation.surface: A magistrate who is forever leaving work before time.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a lazy official, but 'finishing early' is an instruction to cut the last letter of EVER.
annotation.definitionFit: A reeve was a local magistrate or chief officer of a town or district in Anglo-Saxon England.

entries.clue: Startling beat captured by revolutionary recording (7)

indicatorNotes.captured by: the beat is held inside the recording
indicatorNotes.revolutionary: a revolution turns the word round

blocks.note: TAPE reversed to EPAT, opening round the beat
to tan someone's hide is to beat them
the closing letter of the reversed tape

annotation.surface: A startling beat is captured on some revolutionary recording.
annotation.walkthrough: Épatant is French borrowed into English, as in épater les bourgeois. 'Beat' reads as a rhythm on the record, but it is the thrashing sense.
annotation.definitionFit: Épatant means shocking or startling, especially to conventional people.

entries.clue: What led to the growth of cities badly invited rural solution (10,10)

annotation.definition: What led to the growth of cities

indicatorNotes.badly: the letters are put together badly, so rearranged

annotation.surface: Planners invited a rural fix for sprawling cities, and it went badly.
annotation.walkthrough: The fodder's own words, rural and solution, sit well with city growth, which helps hide that they are raw letters. Twenty letters make a long anagram, so crossing letters are worth getting first.
annotation.definitionFit: The Industrial Revolution drew workers from the land into factory towns, causing cities to grow fast.

entries.clue: Guess your setter’s in the commons? (8)

blocks.note: ESTATE: the commons are the third estate of the realm; it opens here
the rest of ESTATE closes round I'M

annotation.surface: A voter asks whether the crossword setter might be sitting in the House of Commons.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Your setter' is how a crossword compiler refers to themself, so it gives I or ME, here I'M. The three estates were clergy, nobles and commons.
annotation.definitionFit: To estimate is to make a rough guess at a value or amount.

entries.clue: Try to hear birds during English fall (9)

indicatorNotes.during: the birds come in the middle of the fall

blocks.note: Aves is the Latin name for the class of birds

annotation.surface: Birdwatchers straining to hear birds during an English autumn.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fall' is the American word for autumn in the surface, but it is a DROP here. AVES comes from biology, the class name for all birds.
annotation.definitionFit: To eavesdrop is to listen in secretly, trying to hear what others say.

entries.clue: Go round one foreign city (5)

indicatorNotes.round: the word for go goes round the one

blocks.note: TURN, a go or go on your turn; it opens here

annotation.surface: Advice to a tourist: go round a single foreign city.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Go' reads as a verb, but it is the noun TURN, as in 'whose go is it?'.
annotation.definitionFit: Turin is a city in north-west Italy, so foreign to a British setter.

entries.clue: Ten images repositioned to make attractive (9)

indicatorNotes.repositioned: the letters are put in new positions

annotation.surface: A designer moves ten pictures around a wall to make it look better.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as interior design, with 'attractive' meaning pretty; the answer takes it in the physical sense of pulling metal.
annotation.definitionFit: To magnetise something is to give it magnetic power, literally making it attractive.

entries.clue: Time to go on social media site with new name (7)

annotation.definition: social media site with new name

blocks.note: to witter is to talk on and on about trivia

annotation.surface: Time to leave the social media site that has been renamed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Go on' reads as 'continue'; here it means to chatter at length. Witter is chiefly British: to prattle pointlessly.
annotation.definitionFit: Twitter was renamed X in 2023, hence 'with new name'.

entries.clue: Is correspondence for him? (6)

annotation.definitionNote: the definition is a pronoun standing for a man's name
annotation.surface: Someone at the door asks whether the post is for a particular man.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Him' is a bare pointer to some man's name, the clue's question mark admitting the looseness. Ismail is a common Muslim given name.
annotation.definitionFit: Ismail is a man's name, the Arabic form of Ishmael, so 'him' can point to him.

entries.clue: Situation confused Bangladesh after boy goes missing (7)

indicatorNotes.confused: the remaining letters are mixed up
indicatorNotes.goes missing: the boy's letters are taken out

annotation.surface: A news report: after a boy vanishes, Bangladesh is in confusion.
annotation.walkthrough: LAD is the crossword's usual boy. Take it out of Bangladesh and the seven letters left make SHEBANG.
annotation.definitionFit: A shebang is a situation or affair, as in 'the whole shebang'.

entries.clue: One attacking a small southern tree of heaven endlessly (9)

indicatorNotes.endlessly: the tree's name loses its ending

blocks.note: S = small, as on clothes labels
AILANTHUS, the tree of heaven, with its ending HUS cut

annotation.surface: Someone attacks a small southern tree of heaven, and keeps on without end.
annotation.walkthrough: The tree of heaven is Ailanthus, a fast-growing Chinese tree common in cities. 'Endlessly' here cuts three letters, which is generous.
annotation.definitionFit: An assailant is one who attacks another.

entries.clue: Tenant of fields and house with tree outside (11)

indicatorNotes.outside: the tree goes outside the house

blocks.note: ELDER, a tree; it opens here

annotation.surface: A tenant farmer rents fields and a house with a tree standing outside.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Of' reads as part of the tenant's description, but it only joins. LEA is a poetic meadow, a crossword staple.
annotation.definitionFit: A leaseholder holds a property on a lease, so is a tenant.

entries.clue: Often finished a new port before answer’s found in a gin (4,3,4,5)

indicatorNotes.before: the pieces so far come ahead of the next
indicatorNotes.found in: the answer's A is placed inside A GIN

blocks.note: A GIN, opening round the answer
the closing letters of A GIN

annotation.surface: Someone often ended up at a new port, a gin in hand before the answer came.
annotation.walkthrough: A long charade in which each word does one small job. Dover is England's main Channel ferry port.
annotation.definitionFit: Over and over again means repeatedly, very often.

entries.clue: Text from college is hardly one that’s entertaining (6)

indicatorNotes.Text from: the answer is lifted from the words that follow

blocks.note: the answer runs from the end of college, through is, into the start of hardly

annotation.surface: A student notes that a college text is hardly entertaining reading.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hardly one that's entertaining' reads as a sneer at the text; the definition is just 'one that's entertaining', and 'hardly' supplies HA.
annotation.definitionFit: A geisha is a Japanese woman trained to entertain guests with music, dance and conversation.

entries.clue: Everything’s as it should be here in a large country, right? (3,7,3,7)

indicatorNotes.in: the word for here sits inside the country

blocks.note: LAND, a country; it opens here
here, as in answering a roll call

annotation.surface: A proud citizen declares all is well in a big country, and asks for agreement.
annotation.walkthrough: The trailing 'right?' reads as a tag question but is the last chunk, CORRECT. The phrase is a military report that all personnel and kit are accounted for.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom from military roll calls and kit inspections, now used of anything found in proper order.

entries.clue: Sign of resistance returning a possible diamond ring (5)

indicatorNotes.returning: the pieces come back, read right to left

blocks.note: a diamond is one kind of gem

annotation.surface: A woman hands back a diamond ring as a sign she resists the proposal.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a refused engagement, but 'resistance' is electrical: the ohm's symbol is the Greek capital omega, Ω.
annotation.definitionFit: Omega (Ω) is the symbol for the ohm, the unit of electrical resistance.

entries.clue: Suspicion mostly to take possession of girl (7)

indicatorNotes.mostly: most of the word is used: its last letter goes

blocks.note: sus, informal British for suspicion, as in 'on sus'
ANNEX, to take possession of, without its last letter

annotation.surface: A jealous suitor's suspicion leads him mostly to want to possess a girl.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mostly' sits between the two pieces and applies to the one after it. Sus is British slang for suspicion, source of the old 'sus law' on stop and search.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: Susanne is one of countless female given names, the kind of vague pointer only crossings pin down.

entries.clue: Stag, elk, skate and civet all essentially are big-mouthed (9)

indicatorNotes.all essentially: the essence, or middle, of each of the four words

blocks.note: the middle two letters of sTAg
the middle three letters of sKATe
the middle three letters of cIVEt

annotation.surface: A naturalist claims that stags, elks, skates and civets all have big mouths.
annotation.walkthrough: The middles are of different lengths, one, two or three letters, which is what makes this hard to spot. 'Big-mouthed' reads as jaws on animals but means chatty.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone big-mouthed talks too much, so is talkative.

entries.clue: Decorator is power finishing before beginning to repaint (9)

blocks.note: last, as in the finishing one
ere is old or poetic for before

annotation.surface: A decorator is energetically finishing the job before starting to repaint.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Before' reads as the order of work, but it is the word ERE. A plasterer's trade is close to a decorator's.
annotation.definitionFit: A plasterer finishes walls and ceilings and can be called a decorator, especially of ornamental plasterwork.

entries.clue: Lack of vigour I intend getting raised in drinkers’ group (7)

indicatorNotes.raised: in a down clue, raised means written upwards
indicatorNotes.in: the turned phrase goes inside the group

blocks.note: AA, Alcoholics Anonymous; it opens here
I MEAN, I intend, turned upwards

annotation.surface: A member of a drinkers' support group plans to raise their lack of energy.
annotation.walkthrough: The drinkers' group is AA, which ironically is for people who have stopped drinking. 'Getting' is part of the reversal instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Anaemia is a lack of red blood cells, and figuratively a lack of vigour or spirit.

entries.clue: Bird’s cry caught greeting noise of cat returning (7)

indicatorNotes.returning: the cat's noise comes back, read right to left

annotation.surface: A bird's cry, caught when it greets a cat that has come back purring.
annotation.walkthrough: C for caught comes from cricket scorecards. The cat purring back into the scene becomes a reversed PURR.
annotation.definitionFit: A chirrup is a bird's short chirping cry.

entries.clue: Boasted less than attractive hair style (7)

indicatorNotes.less than: the word falls short of its full length by a letter

blocks.note: crew is an old past tense of crow, to boast
CUTE, attractive, less its last letter

annotation.surface: Someone boasted about a hairstyle that was less than attractive.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Less than attractive' reads as mildly ugly, but it means CUTE short of a letter. CREW as a past tense of crow is now rare outside the cock that crew.
annotation.definitionFit: A crew cut is a very short, bristly hair style.

entries.clue: Droppings round horse’s back absorbing upper-class (5)

indicatorNotes.back: the horse word is read backwards
indicatorNotes.absorbing: the turned word takes in U

blocks.note: NAG, a horse, turned to GAN; it opens here
U = upper-class, as in 'U and non-U' English

annotation.surface: Manure spread round a horse's rear, soaking up some posh stuff.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Horse's back' reads as the animal's rear, but it is NAG read back. 'Round' leads the clue yet its O lands last.
annotation.definitionFit: Guano is the droppings of seabirds or bats, used as fertiliser.

entries.clue: Sleep during sex is not appropriate (5)

indicatorNotes.during: the sleep comes in the middle of sex

blocks.note: IT, crossword slang for sex; it opens here

annotation.surface: Nodding off in bed at the wrong moment is not appropriate.
annotation.walkthrough: IT for sex (or sex appeal) is an old slang use the crossword keeps alive.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the prefix IN- negates APT, just as NOT negates appropriate.

entries.clue: One supporting swine with swine supporting them initially (7)

indicatorNotes.initially: what comes initially is what comes first, so only the first letter of them is used
indicatorNotes.supporting: in a down clue, the swine is written below T, holding it up

blocks.note: the second swine: a rotter, a nasty person; supporting puts it beneath T

annotation.surface: A riddle about pigs holding each other up.
annotation.walkthrough: The two swines differ: the first is a pig, whose feet support it; the second is a person, a rotter. In a down clue, supporting means placed underneath.
annotation.definitionFit: A trotter is a pig's foot, which supports the animal.

entries.clue: Arrest — surprisingly resistance happened (9)

indicatorNotes.surprisingly: the letters come out in an unexpected order

annotation.surface: An arrest was made; surprisingly, there was resistance.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a police report, and resistance fits an arrest so well that R is easy to miss as a letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym from police language, where apprehending a suspect means seizing them.

entries.clue: Fabric printer’s measure, one coming in 500 metres (5)

indicatorNotes.coming in: the measure and the one go inside

blocks.note: D = 500 in Roman numerals; D M opens here
an en is a printer's unit of width
M = metres, closing round EN and I

annotation.surface: A printer measures out fabric, one piece arriving in a 500-metre roll.
annotation.walkthrough: '500 metres' looks like a length of cloth, but it splits into D (Roman 500) and M (metres). The printer's measures are EM and EN.
annotation.definitionFit: Denim is the tough cotton twill fabric used for jeans.

entries.clue: Extremely happy former partner dealt with changes (7)

indicatorNotes.changes: the letters of dealt are changed around

annotation.surface: Someone is delighted that their ex has dealt with some changes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dealt with changes' reads as coping; 'with' only joins, and 'changes' tells you to shuffle DEALT.
annotation.definitionFit: Exalted can mean elated, in a state of extreme happiness.

entries.clue: Champion keeping school solvent (7)

indicatorNotes.keeping: the champion holds the school inside

blocks.note: ACE, a champion; it opens here
Eton College, the English public school

annotation.surface: A champion keeps her school financially solvent.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Solvent' reads as out of debt; it is the chemical sense. Eton is the crossword's default school.
annotation.definitionFit: Acetone is a common solvent, used in nail-varnish remover.

entries.clue: Result of pressing investigation — shells perhaps covered in minute chickpeas? (9)

indicatorNotes.covered in: the shells go inside the minute

blocks.note: shells are one kind of ammunition
gram is the Indian name for chickpeas

annotation.surface: A cook covers shells with tiny chickpeas after pressing them.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pressing' reads as urgent, but a mammogram is taken while the breast is pressed between plates. Gram is the chickpea in Indian cooking, as in gram flour.
annotation.definitionFit: A mammogram is the X-ray image from a breast examination done by compressing the breast.

entries.clue: Silently contemplated sea engulfing you and me (5)

indicatorNotes.engulfing: the sea swallows you and me

blocks.note: MED, the Mediterranean; it opens here

annotation.surface: Staring quietly at a sea wave that might swallow the two of us.
annotation.walkthrough: The sea here is the Med, the common short form of the Mediterranean.
annotation.definitionFit: To muse is to think quietly and at length, so mused means silently contemplated.

entries.clue: Spice island stripped fennec pelt (7,6)

indicatorNotes.stripped: the fox's outer letters are stripped off

blocks.note: a cay is a low island or reef
to pepper is to pelt with shot or missiles

annotation.surface: An island trader sells spice and a fennec fox's stripped pelt.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pelt' reads as a fur, which fits the fox, but it is the verb, to bombard. A fennec is a small big-eared desert fox.
annotation.definitionFit: Cayenne pepper is a hot spice made from ground chillies.

entries.clue: Unknown typefaces including Roman capital can be pants (1-6)

indicatorNotes.including: to include is to hold within, so the typefaces take R inside them

annotation.surface: A designer complains that unknown typefaces, even Roman capitals, can be pants.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pants' in the surface is British slang for rubbish; in the answer it means underpants. 'Roman capital' reads as a typeface style but is the first letter of Roman.
annotation.definitionFit: Y-fronts are men's briefs with a Y-shaped front seam; in Britain, pants are underpants.

entries.clue: Dog secured by lead — better late than never? (7)

indicatorNotes.secured by: the dog is held inside the lead

blocks.note: PB, the chemical symbol for lead; it opens here
a stock name for a dog

annotation.surface: Putting a dog on its lead: better late than never.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lead' is a dog's leash in the surface but the metal Pb here. The definition is an example, hence the question mark.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Better late than never' is a well-known proverb.

entries.clue: Caller chasing good state nurse (6,7)

indicatorNotes.chasing: the caller comes behind the good state

annotation.surface: A caller pursues a nurse employed by the good state.
annotation.walkthrough: In Britain a health visitor is a community nurse who visits families at home, especially those with babies. 'Chasing' puts VISITOR second.
annotation.definitionFit: A health visitor is a nurse who visits people in their homes.

entries.clue: Manually produced pair of taps, judged about fine (11)

indicatorNotes.about: the judged word goes round fine

blocks.note: H and C, the hot and cold taps

annotation.surface: A plumber's pair of hand-made taps was judged about fine.
annotation.walkthrough: The pair of taps is literally H AND C, the hot and cold labels, so the word AND comes free.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: manual comes from the Latin for hand, so manually produced is crafted by hand.

entries.clue: What beats transport system old men reconstructed (9)

indicatorNotes.reconstructed: the letters of old men are rebuilt in a new order

annotation.surface: Old men rebuilt a transport system that beats anything else.
annotation.walkthrough: 'What beats' reads as a boast; it means a device that ticks out beats. Old is O.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic-flavoured description: the device ticks out a steady pulse, so it is literally the thing that beats.

entries.clue: Modern teen’s involved record of lawbreaking (11)

annotation.surface: A modern teenager is involved in some offence on their record.
annotation.walkthrough: In Britain an endorsement is a note of a driving offence put on your licence, along with penalty points.
annotation.definitionFit: An endorsement on a driving licence records a traffic offence.

entries.clue: One not taking sides, nervous about end of conflict (7)

indicatorNotes.about: the nervous word goes round the letter

blocks.note: NEURAL, of the nerves; it opens here

annotation.surface: A neutral country is nervous about how a conflict will end.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Nervous' reads as anxious; here it means to do with nerves, NEURAL.
annotation.definitionFit: A neutral is a person or state that takes no side in a conflict.

entries.clue: Stubbs maybe finished — in the end had to keep roan’s head simple (9)

annotation.type: charade + container + first letter + last letter

indicatorNotes.in the end: the end of a word is its last letter, so only the final D of had is used
indicatorNotes.to keep: the finished word holds roan's first letter
indicatorNotes.head: a head sits at the top, so roan's head is its first letter

annotation.surface: George Stubbs finished his painting of a roan horse in a simple style.
annotation.walkthrough: Stubbs and roan conjure George Stubbs, the horse painter, but the Stubbs meant is Una Stubbs, a British TV actress. 'Maybe' flags her as one example of a Stubbs.
annotation.definitionFit: Unadorned means plain, without decoration, so simple.

entries.clue: Party dress to discard, one going with black attire (9)

blocks.note: to can something is to scrap it

annotation.surface: Advice to throw out a party frock and go in black instead.
annotation.walkthrough: The Dominicans are the Black Friars, named for their black cloaks; London's Blackfriars is named after them.
annotation.definitionFit: A Dominican friar wears a black mantle over a white habit.

entries.clue: French writer meaning to get translated (9)

indicatorNotes.translated: the letters are carried over into a new form

annotation.surface: A French writer whose meaning is to be translated.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Translated' fits a French writer perfectly, which hides that it is only shuffling the letters of 'meaning to'.
annotation.definitionFit: Michel de Montaigne was the sixteenth-century French essayist.

entries.clue: What helps people get on university course (9)

blocks.note: the rapport between people who click

annotation.surface: Something that helps students get ahead at university.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Get on' reads as succeed, but it means get along with each other.
annotation.definitionFit: Chemistry is both the attraction between people and a science taught at university.

entries.clue: Make improvements to staff editor retains (5)

indicatorNotes.retains: the editor keeps the staff inside

blocks.note: ED, an editor, opening round the staff

annotation.surface: An editor keeps on the staff, making improvements to them.
annotation.walkthrough: Staff here is people, MEN, not a stick. The editor is the usual ED.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym used of texts: editors emend a manuscript by correcting it.

entries.clue: Pandemonium as Charles embraces Oscar (5)

blocks.note: CHAS, short for Charles, opening round Oscar

annotation.surface: Uproar breaks out when Charles hugs an Oscar winner.
annotation.walkthrough: Chas is the written short form of Charles. Oscar is O in the radio alphabet.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: Milton coined Pandemonium as the capital of Hell, and the word now means wild uproar.

entries.clue: Certain to limit tattoo’s size? (7)

indicatorNotes.to limit: the certain word goes round the tattoo, hemming it in

annotation.surface: A tattooist is sure to keep a tattoo's size down.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tat' is informal for a tattoo. The 's only joins it to the definition, which is 'size', with a question mark for the looseness.
annotation.definitionFit: Stature is a person's height, their bodily size.

entries.clue: News — it is interrupted by Scottish strike (7)

blocks.note: to ding is Scots for to strike

annotation.surface: A news flash: a Scottish strike has interrupted things.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Strike' suggests industrial action; here it is a blow, the Scots verb ding.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, though tidings is the older, literary word, as in 'good tidings of great joy'.

entries.clue: Look down on little sister holding on to papa in river (7)

indicatorNotes.in: the whole lot sits in the river

blocks.note: DEE, a river; it opens here
SIS, short for sister; it opens round P

annotation.surface: A little sister clings to dad in the river, looking down on the rest.
annotation.walkthrough: Two containers nest: P inside SIS, then SPIS inside DEE. The Dee is a river in Scotland and another on the Welsh border.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: despise comes from Latin despicere, literally to look down.

entries.clue: Royal weapon of unknown calibre set in a lot of gems all over (9)

indicatorNotes.a lot of: most of the word: its last letter goes
indicatorNotes.all over: the gems word is turned over, read backwards
indicatorNotes.set in: the unknown and calibre are set inside

blocks.clueFragment: a lot of gems all over
blocks.note: RUBIE(S) reversed to EIBUR; it opens here

blocks.clueFragment: a lot of gems all over
blocks.note: EIBUR closes round X and CAL

annotation.surface: A royal weapon of unknown bore is set among a hoard of gems.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Calibre' fits a weapon so well it hides that it only gives the abbreviation CAL.
annotation.definitionFit: Excalibur is King Arthur's sword, a royal weapon.

entries.clue: Burning smell around one type of battery? (7)

annotation.definitionNote: the answer is a metal used to name a battery type, hence the question mark

indicatorNotes.around: the smell goes around the one

blocks.note: HUM, a bad smell; it opens here

annotation.surface: A burning smell comes from around a battery.
annotation.walkthrough: Hum is British slang for a bad smell. The surface of an overheating battery is apt for lithium cells.
annotation.definitionFit: Lithium batteries, including lithium-ion, are named after the metal.

entries.clue: A god turned insect? Almost freakish (9)

indicatorNotes.turned: the god's name is turned round
indicatorNotes.Almost: the insect falls one letter short

annotation.surface: A god transformed into an insect: nearly bizarre enough to be myth.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Turned' sounds like a transformation, but it only reverses AMON. The question mark after 'insect' hides that 'Almost' begins a new instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Anomalous means abnormal or irregular, so freakish.

entries.clue: Workshop I later rebuilt to conserve energy (7)

indicatorNotes.rebuilt: the letters are built into a new order
indicatorNotes.to conserve: the jumble keeps the E inside it

blocks.note: E = energy, kept inside the mix

annotation.surface: An owner says he later rebuilt his workshop to save energy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Conserve energy' reads as green building, but it tells you to hold E in the anagram.
annotation.definitionFit: An atelier is a workshop or studio, especially an artist's or designer's.

entries.clue: Exclusive landed in middle of week (5)

blocks.note: the middle letters of wEEk, EE; it opens here
a bird lit on a branch

annotation.surface: An exclusive flight that landed in the middle of the week.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Landed' reads as a plane arriving, or as landed gentry; it is LIT, past tense of light, to settle.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym used as an adjective, as in an elite club open only to a chosen few.

entries.clue: Part of painting exhibiting slight colouration (5)

indicatorNotes.Part of: the answer is only part of the words
indicatorNotes.exhibiting: the words put the answer on show

blocks.note: the answer straddles the gap: the end of painting and the start of exhibiting

annotation.surface: An art critic notes that part of a painting shows a faint tint.
annotation.walkthrough: The painting surface fits the definition so well that the hidden word sits in plain sight.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a faint tint laid over something, as in a blue tinge.

entries.clue: Elbow groom into picture — but there’s no room (5)

indicatorNotes.but there’s no room: with no room left in it, the groom loses the letters ROOM
indicatorNotes.into: what is left goes into the picture

blocks.note: NUDE, a painting of a naked figure, opening round the groom
GROOM minus ROOM, since there's no room

annotation.surface: Elbowing a groom into the wedding photo when there's no room.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a crowded wedding photo, and 'no room' is also an instruction: take ROOM out of GROOM to leave G.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym as verbs: a dig with the elbow is exactly what a nudge is.

entries.clue: Language feature associated with Oxford? (6)

blocks.note: a language, as in the one you learn at your mother's knee
an Oxford is a lace-up shoe; think of the flap under its laces

annotation.surface: A linguistic feature linked with Oxford, perhaps its accent.
annotation.walkthrough: Oxford suggests the university and its English; here it is an Oxford shoe, a classic lace-up, and the tongue is the flap under the laces.
annotation.definitionFit: A tongue is a language, and also the flap under a shoe's laces.

entries.clue: I note golf might be derived from this kids’ game? (5,2,3,6)

annotation.definition: I note golf might be derived from this kids’ game?

blocks.clueFragment: I note golf might be derived from
blocks.note: the surface: some sport grew out of a playground game
the meaning: the letter in the middle of the word PIGGY is G, which is golf in the NATO alphabet

annotation.surface: A sports historian muses that golf might have grown out of a children's game.
annotation.walkthrough: Read the answer literally: what is in the middle of PIGGY? Its third letter, G, and G is golf in the radio alphabet. Piggy in the middle is a game where one child tries to intercept a ball thrown over them.
annotation.definitionFit: Piggy in the middle is a children's ball game, and literally the middle of PIGGY is G for golf.

entries.clue: Avoid motorway in bumpy vehicle (6)

annotation.surface: Advice to avoid the motorway when travelling in a bumpy old car.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In' reads as travelling inside the vehicle, but it only joins. British motorways are numbered M1, M25 and so on. A dodgem is a bumper car.
annotation.definitionFit: A dodgem is a fairground bumper car, built for bumping.

entries.clue: Consecrated ground church gauge the ultimate in holy (8)

indicatorNotes.the ultimate in: ultimate means last, so the ultimate in holy is its last letter

annotation.surface: A churchyard said to be the last word in holiness.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The ultimate in holy' reads as the height of sanctity, but it means its last letter. CE is the Church of England.
annotation.definitionFit: A description: a burial ground is blessed, or consecrated, before the dead are laid in it.

entries.clue: Storm as English politician appears in trial (7)

indicatorNotes.appears in: the English politician shows up inside the trial

blocks.note: TEST, a trial, opening round the politician
TEST closes round E and MP

annotation.surface: Uproar as an English MP turns up in court.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Storm' reads as a verb, to storm out, but it is the noun, a tempest.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, the literary word for a violent storm, as in Shakespeare's play.
